title: A Small Rebellion
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 33 of 40
content:
The official arrived at the Jasmine Dragon before the lunch rush and demanded the best table.

I knew he was an official because he told us twice before he had taken three steps past the door.

His boots were polished, his coat bore a city inspection seal, and the younger clerk following him looked profoundly uncomfortable. There were four ordinary customers ahead of them, including an old woman who had been waiting for hot water since the morning rain.

Iroh bowed from behind the counter.

"Welcome. How may we help?"

"Inspector Han," the man said. "I am here to review the premises. I will take tea while your staff prepare the records."

"Of course. The public inspection record is available in the office. We can begin with it after the current customers have been served."

Han looked at the waiting line.

"I don't stand in lines."

I felt my shoulders tighten.

Iroh's expression did not change.

"A useful thing to know about you," he said pleasantly. "You may prefer the empty chair by the window while we finish."

The old woman covered a smile with her hand.

Han's clerk looked at the floor.

I wanted to say something sharp. I wanted to tell Han that the city had changed, that nobody could order a man like Iroh around in his own shop, that people who used titles as weapons deserved to be embarrassed.

The problem was that Han might have legitimate inspection work to do. I wanted to protect the customers without turning the room into another battle over who held the greater authority.

I stepped beside Iroh.

"Which records do you need first?" I asked.

Han looked at me.

"The kitchen sanitation log. Temperature records. Ingredient storage."

"We have those. Would you like the current public sheet or the full inspection file?"

His expression shifted.

"The full file."

"Then we can bring it to the office table after Mina finishes serving. The staff can answer questions about the work they actually perform."

Han looked impatient.

"Do you own this shop?"

"I help here," I said. "Iroh is the proprietor. Mina manages much of the morning service."

He turned back to Iroh.

"Then perhaps the proprietor should answer."

Iroh smiled.

"The proprietor is listening."

For a moment I thought Han might order the shop closed just because he disliked being contradicted. The clerk behind him cleared her throat.

"Inspector, the posted inspection protocol says we should begin with the existing log. The serving queue isn't part of the review."

Han looked at her.

She stood very straight.

"Thank you, Clerk Ren," Iroh said. "That is helpful."

Ren looked relieved.

Mina brought the tea to the waiting customers, then took the sanitation log from beneath the counter. She had kept the last three weeks' entries in tidy columns, including a note where the back storage shelf had been moved to keep it dry during a leak.

Han examined the page.

"This shelf was moved without my approval."

Mina set down her tray.

"It was moved away from water during an emergency. We logged the change and asked the building steward to inspect the new placement."

"Where is the inspection?"

She opened the next page.

"Here."

Han studied it, then glanced toward the back corridor.

"I will need to see the shelf."

"Of course," Iroh said.

Mina led the way. I followed at a respectful distance, leaving Iroh to manage the front room. The inspection was tedious rather than dramatic. Han measured the distance between storage jars and the wall. Ren checked the seal dates. Mina answered every question without pretending a kitchen stayed safe just because it belonged to a beloved proprietor.

One jar had been labeled poorly.

Han pointed it out.

"That must be corrected."

Mina nodded.

"Agreed. I'll relabel it before service."

Iroh, who had come to hear the result, looked almost pleased.

"Thank you for noticing."

Han blinked.

He had expected a fight.

He did not get one.

Back at the counter, however, he insisted that his tea should be free as a courtesy to his office.

Iroh put down the receipt.

"Our inspection is a public responsibility," he said. "The tea is a private purchase."

"You are making this difficult."

"I am making the difference clear."

I looked toward Ren. She had gone pale.

"Does the city reimburse meals for inspectors?" I asked.

"No," she said quietly.

"Then we can provide the bill in the usual way."

Han stared at the counter for a long moment.

Then he paid.

It was not a triumphant victory. He left with a list of two legitimate corrections and one question about a ventilation grate that required further review. The shop would have to make those repairs, because safety rules applied even when an inspector behaved badly.

Mina leaned against the wall after the door closed.

"That was exhausting," she said.

Iroh handed her a cup.

"Then please sit."

She stared.

"I'm on shift."

"You have been dealing with officials for an hour. The next orders can wait three minutes."

She sat.

Ren returned unexpectedly, alone, carrying a corrected receipt for the inspection fee. She looked nervous.

"Inspector Han forgot to give you this," she said.

"Thank you," I said.

She hesitated.

"I wanted to apologize for how he spoke to the staff. It wasn't appropriate."

Mina considered.

"Then please tell him that."

Ren looked surprised.

"I will."

She left before anybody asked her to become a symbol of the whole city.

Mina came back before anyone could declare the inspection finished. She carried a charcoal sketch of the kitchen flue.

“The smoke pulls backward when we close the east window,” she said. “Winter will make that a problem.”

Iroh turned the sketch sideways. His posture changed; the shopkeeper gave way to someone who had once calculated siege lines and escape routes. “We can move the intake.”

“Onto my prep counter?” Mina asked.

He looked again. “Perhaps not.”

His second suggestion blocked the delivery path. His third would have cost more than the week's food budget.

“You're planning the room as though nobody works in it,” I said.

For a long moment he looked offended. Then he passed the charcoal to Mina.

“Show me where the work actually happens.”

She did. He listened, made notes, and asked her to choose a contractor she'd trust to inspect the flue. He also asked whether she wanted paid time for the appointment. She said yes without apology.

Later I caught him staring at the drawing.

“Your former soldiers didn't argue this much, did they?”

“Some did,” he said. “They were generally the ones who kept us alive.”

It was a sharper answer than his usual teasing. I liked him better for it. He wasn't always serene; sometimes he disliked being contradicted and chose to listen anyway.

The kettle shrieked in the next room. Mina called for the fresh pot. Iroh folded the drawing, went to fetch the tea, and left the contractor's decision where it belonged.


After the lunch rush, Iroh and I stood in the pantry, where the air smelled of dried peel and jasmine. I had been carrying an ache behind my ribs since Han first walked through the door.

"Are you angry?" I asked.

"Yes."

"At him?"

"At the assumption that power exists to make other people smaller."

I looked at him.

"You could have frightened him."

"I know."

"Did you want to?"

He considered.

"For a moment, yes."

I leaned against the shelf.

"Thank you for not turning the whole room into a lesson about your former rank."

He smiled sadly.

"I would like the shop to belong to the people who use it. Not to the general I used to be."

I touched his hand.

We had spoken plainly about my ethical non-monogamy and preference for polyamory. He understood that I did not enter his life to become a trophy of his redemption or a replacement for anyone he had lost. We came together because we could choose what kind of ordinary day we wanted to share.

"Can I kiss you?" I asked.

"That would improve the afternoon considerably."

I kissed him, then laughed when he caught a loose strand of my hair against the shelf. He untangled it carefully.

The next customer called for jasmine tea.

Iroh looked toward the door.

"Your turn," he said.

I stepped to the counter and took the order.

That evening we updated the storage labels and scheduled the ventilation inspection. Mina signed the correction sheet, and Iroh paid the repair deposit from the actual shop budget.

The inspector's bad manners did not make his safety concerns imaginary.

The repair cost was not a punishment.

It was the price of keeping a place where people could rest without needing a title.

When we locked the shop, Iroh offered his arm. I took it. We went upstairs with the day behind us, not defeated, not magically solved, but ours.
